posts.body_html:
Thanks for the clarification, Nico! Indeed, this clone is F25C, and I think I remember Mike King explaining to me that he also believes this is the original clone.

It's rather interesting to see how it looks in many different collections. Here, it looks like an ornata. While I find this plant rather beautiful and shapely, it's surprising how popular it is in Europe. Many other clones consistently have more intense colors-perhaps the history of this clone has something to do with it?

posts.body_html:
you welcome, Mike.
How about the plant, looks different because of the different climates here in europe; in southern Italy pitchers start up to january, and colors are very intense compared to the same plant, but in a different climate.
For example, my S. x "Crimson Queen" is very much colored than the same plant grown by my friend in Milano.
Adrian Slack observed a seedling in the wild of Sarracenia flava var. rubricorpora 'Claret' and used this plant for the european production of S. 'Claret', very probably by seeds.
this is the description:

Description: Insect-Eat.Pl. & How to Grow Them:71 (1986)
+ "In the ' Red Forms ' (of [Sarracenia flava {L.}]) almost the entire
+ outside of the pitcher is coloured red to maroon, while the inner
+ surface and nectar roll is yellowish green to yellow. In shade the red
+ becomes paler, and strong red veins are then evident. Two good forms
+ which have found their way into cultivation are [Sarracenia ' Burgundy '
+ {Hort.Slack}](...); and [Sarracenia ' Claret ' {Hort.Slack}] is
+ attractive, too, with long slender pitchers tinted maroon and strongly
+ veined in darker colour, giving way to the yellowish-green background
+ color towards the mouth and in the hood. I was shown a pure stand of
+ this form extending to many acres in the Florida Panhandle. This was
+ scheduled for drainage and afforestation, and I believe the solitary
+ seedling which I rescued at the time has been the source of all European
+ stock. (footnote:) [Sarracenia ' Burgundy ' {Hort.Slack}] and
+ [Sarracenia ' Claret ' {Hort.Slack}] are names of convenience applied by
+ the author."

at that times concept of cultivar was different from what we understand it today. the one that seems to be the true S. 'Claret' regarding the cultivar description is F25C MK clone.

There are some clone in europe. one of the most spectacular i've seen is the one grown by my friend Faunista, this is he's plant, obtained as S. 'Claret' by a belgian collector, it has no codes.




this is my F25C MK, two years ago:



F25C MK by Pandalf



if you want, I can link you some other photos of other clones.

posts.body_html:
Wow, that clone grown by Faunista is amazing! 'Claret' is indeed very mysterious, and it makes me wonder if all the "different" clones out there are genetically identical, but have a different phenotype based on environmental conditions.

No doubt, the clone I have is genetically identical to the ones you and Pandalf are growing, but they all look so different!

It's not surprising though...some varieties are more variable than others based on environment. S. leucophylla Hurricane Creek White, for example, can have pitchers of both different shapes and different colors on the same exact clone.

It seems as though many Sarracenia vary in physical appearance from one year to the next, but some individual plants are more extreme than others.

posts.body_html:
hi Mike!
Yes, environmental conditions are important, but there are also other factors to consider.
first of all:the health of the plant. An healthy plant has much color and strenght, obviously.
The second factor is the time the plant has been in a pot with the same substrate and the conditions of this; in facts, plants non-repotted every year are much vigorous and healthy, so we can note much color and taller pitcher the next year! another important factor is the water temperature and its quality. a cold water is always good, plants will grow taller pitcher and roots will be white and healthy! I use large pot saucers in wood and polystyrene to ensure always fresh water! in addition to this the substrate will be always fresh so we don't need to repot every year. in cold temperatures fungi such as Pythium develop much less, peat deteriorates less rapidly! Another factor that i consider is the composition of the substrate: I use a multilayer substrate, on the bottom using only one inch of sponge; after (going up) i use peat quartz sand, perlite and chopped bark for other 2 inch; finally i put peat, perlite and quartz sand. if i got it, i'll put live sphagnum. in the coming years I will replace the peat with coconut fiber, in my small way, I want to preserve peat bogs, where carnivorous plants grow. I use also pots made ​​from various plastics, making them by similar to an hydroponic pot.
Another factor to consider is catches of the plant: more catches, more is healthy!
another is climate factor: cold night and warm days make the plant much colorful, the greenhouse is also another important factor: with her, plants grow very much faster!
it is not only a plant in a pot that we have to see, but a set of many factors and passion that make the difference!
sometimes it happens that we see very different pitcher from the same rhizome, but we have to think that the plant does not print pitchers like a photocopier!
Ciao!

posts.body_html:
A friend of mine has a 'Claret' of sorts. The plant was a seedling produced at Marston Exotics post Adrian Slack and purchased as such during a visit to the UK in the 1990s. There is some question as to whether the seedlings were labelled by the nursery as cv S.'Claret'.

So, while technically not the "cultivar" it is very, very similar and could easily be confused for Mike King's clone F25C though it 100% is not. My friend's clone, a real beauty in its own right, is correctly not labelled as S.'Claret'. As you guys have pointed out, clones can be highly variable in and of themselves without the added complication of misidentification!! Certainly nico and Mike, at a similar stage of development your clones appear quite different from my friend's one and Pandalf's.

If you look closely at the photos below you'll notice the clone I refer to has a notably long terminal spur - much longer than the other clones in question including those grown by Mike King. Possibly this one is better? Guess that's in the eye of the beholder

In fact, any "Claret" presents as almost intermediate between var. ornata and var. rubricorpora. Without the red flush it would be an excellent ornata.

Here are some nice pics taken by my friend in his greenhouse. The first two are the freshly opened but mostly fully formed pitchers while last photo is of the same clone taken 50 days after the first ones.

posts.body_html:
What a strange looking hood on the past two photos-that's a neat clone!

Adrian slack ran Marston exotics, right? If that's true, and the description that Nico stated above that only one seedling of Claret was collected, it would imply that all of our clones either are that individual or are offspring from it.

The rubricorporas near Sumatra, Liberty Co, FL look distinctly different from claret and the one KiwiEarl has from Marston Exotics. Typically, it seems as though flavas from the carolinas have a higher frequency of individuals longer terminal spurs than flavas in the panhandle, which makes me really confused as to the origin of Claret. However, what exists to day in the panhandle is only an iota of what was there in the past, so it's quite possible that there were huge populations of long spured flavas that are extinct today.
